title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
summary: A compact array-based structure for O(log n) prefix-sum queries and point/range updates in a fraction of a segment tree's code.

slides.markdown:
A **Fenwick tree** (binary indexed tree, BIT) answers the same core question as a segment tree — prefix sums and point updates in O(log n) — using a single flat array and a bit-manipulation trick instead of an explicit recursive tree structure. For sum-like operations specifically, it's the leaner tool: less code, smaller constant factor, and conceptually simpler once the indexing trick clicks.

The trade is real, though: a Fenwick tree leans on the operation being **invertible** (subtraction undoes addition), which sum has and min/max/gcd don't — that's exactly the gap the previous topic's segment tree fills for those cases.

slides.subTitle: How index & (-index) encodes the tree's implicit structure
slides.markdown:
A Fenwick tree has no explicit parent/child pointers — its structure is implicit, encoded entirely in binary arithmetic on indices. The key operation is `index & (-index)` (in two's complement, this isolates the **lowest set bit** of `index`), often called "lowbit."

Each array slot `i` in the Fenwick tree stores the sum of a specific range: the `lowbit(i)` elements ending at index `i`. To move to the next index that needs updating when index `i` changes, add `lowbit(i)` to `i`. To move to the previous range needed when querying a prefix sum up to index `i`, subtract `lowbit(i)` from `i`. These two moves — add lowbit to update, subtract lowbit to query — are the entire algorithm.

slides.subTitle: In a few lines each
Why the structure assumes 1-indexing
slides.markdown:
The lowbit trick specifically breaks at index 0: `0 & (-0)` is 0, so the update/query loop would never terminate (or never even start moving) if index 0 were treated as a valid Fenwick index. This is why Fenwick trees are conventionally **1-indexed** internally, even when the underlying problem's array is naturally 0-indexed.

The practical fix is a small, consistent offset: when the caller's array is 0-indexed, map external index `i` to internal Fenwick index `i + 1` at every call site (`update(i, delta)` becomes `update(i + 1, delta)`), and keep that offset applied consistently everywhere the tree is touched — mixing 0-indexed and 1-indexed calls in the same codebase is a common, hard-to-spot source of off-by-one bugs in Fenwick tree code specifically.

slides.sectionTitle: Range sum query as a difference of two prefix sums
slides.markdown:
The sum over `[l, r]` is `prefix_sum(r) - prefix_sum(l - 1)` — the same telescoping idea behind prefix-sum arrays generally, just computed via the Fenwick tree's O(log n) prefix-sum function instead of an O(1) precomputed array lookup.

This is precisely where sum's invertibility earns its keep: subtracting `prefix_sum(l-1)` correctly "removes" everything before `l`, because addition and subtraction are exact inverses. The equivalent move for **min**, e.g. "min over `[l, r]` equals min over `[0, r]` minus min over `[0, l-1]`" — simply isn't a valid identity, since you can't reliably "un-min" a value the way you can "un-add" one. That's the concrete reason range-min queries need a genuinely different structure (a segment tree) rather than a Fenwick-tree adaptation.

slides.subTitle: Flipping the trick with a difference array
slides.markdown:
The basic Fenwick tree above supports point update + range query. The mirror-image capability — **range update** (add val to every element from l to r) + **point query** (what's the value at a single index) — is achieved with a small transformation: maintain a Fenwick tree over the array's **difference array** (`diff[i] = arr[i] - arr[i-1]`) instead of the array itself.

A range update "add val to `[l, r]`" becomes exactly two point updates on the difference array: `diff[l] += val` and `diff[r+1] -= val` (if `r+1` is in bounds) — the same telescoping trick used for range-update tricks on plain arrays. A point query for `arr[i]` becomes a **prefix sum** up to `i` on the difference array, since summing a difference array's prefix reconstructs the original value at that position.

slides.subTitle: The two-BIT trick for full generality
Less code and lower constant factor vs more query flexibility
slides.markdown:
| | Fenwick tree | Segment tree |
|---|---|---|
| Code size | small — one array, bit tricks | larger — recursive build/query/update |
| Constant factor | lower | higher |
| Works for min/max/gcd | no, not naturally | yes |
| Range update + range query | needs the two-BIT trick | needs lazy propagation, one structure |

Both are correct O(log n) choices for sum-like range problems; the deciding factor is almost always whether the operation is invertible. If it is (sum, XOR), Fenwick trees are usually the leaner, faster-to-write choice. If it isn't (min, max, gcd), a segment tree is close to mandatory — a Fenwick tree simply doesn't have a natural adaptation for those operations.

slides.sectionTitle: When a Fenwick tree is the right-sized tool
slides.subTitle: Sum/count range problems without needing min/max
slides.markdown:
The practical decision rule that closes out both this topic and the previous one: reach for a Fenwick tree by default whenever the problem is genuinely sum-or-count shaped (running totals, frequency counts, inversion counting via sum-of-ranks) and doesn't need range-min/max — it's less code, faster in practice, and easier to get right under time pressure than a segment tree.

Reach for a segment tree the moment any of three things is true: the aggregate operation isn't invertible (min, max, gcd), the problem needs range update **and** range query simultaneously with a non-sum operation, or the combine logic is genuinely custom (not one of the standard associative operations a Fenwick tree's arithmetic trick can absorb). Knowing this decision rule — rather than defaulting to whichever structure you memorized more recently — is the actual signal a strong candidate demonstrates when this topic comes up as a design choice rather than a fixed prompt.
